title: Export worker buffers every row of every table in memory and is OOM-killed on any real-sized library
what: readTables() loops the tenant's public tables and runs `const res = await client.query(`SELECT * FROM "${name}"`)` with no LIMIT, no OFFSET and no server-side cursor, pushing the full result set into a JS array (`out.push({ name, columns, rows, numericColumns })`). The MAX_EXPORT_ROWS = 2_000_000 guard (line 26) is evaluated at line 389 — AFTER the table has already been fully materialised — so it protects nothing. For xlsx the rows are then materialised a second time inside ExcelJS (buildWorkbook), and for the `all` scope this repeats per tenant into one zip.
impact: The worker container (`WORKER_MEM_LIMIT: 1g`, infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:269, no --max-old-space-size) is OOM-killed the first time an Institutional-sized library clicks 'Export'. Everything else the worker owns dies with it: the email outbox queue, in-flight CSV/XLSX imports, and all nine cron sweeps. The export job row is left `running` forever because the failure path never executes. And if the box did have the RAM, the 2M-row cap then aborts the export outright — so the largest paying tier can never export its own data (the product sells data export; GDPR Art. 20 portability rests on it).
evidence: RAN, against a tenant DB seeded to the Institutional numbers the pricing sells (400,000 books / 520,000 copies / 100,000 members / 2,000,000 loans / 3,000,000 audit rows, 1479 MB): a faithful replica of readTables() printed `baseline RSS 81 MB` then `audit_log: 3000000 rows in 4409ms — RSS now 1443 MB, cumulative rows 3000000` then `!! MAX_EXPORT_ROWS (2000000) exceeded AFTER buffering — export ABORTS`. Final `heapUsed 1275 MB`. One table alone, on the first iteration, exceeded the 1 GB container limit. Table sizes measured with pg_total_relation_size: audit_log 609 MB, loans 413 MB, books 168 MB.
fix: Stream instead of buffer. Either add `pg-cursor` and read each table in 10k-row chunks straight into the CSV/JSON/XLSX writer (ExcelJS has a streaming workbook writer, `ExcelJS.stream.xlsx.WorkbookWriter`), or use `COPY (SELECT * FROM t) TO STDOUT WITH CSV` via `pg-copy-streams` piped into the archive. Move the row-count check to a cheap `SELECT reltuples` pre-flight so an oversized export is refused before any work, not after 1.4 GB of allocation. Keep the hard cap only as a backstop.
verification: RAN an independent replica of readTables() against libriant_scale (the same 400k/520k/100k/2M/3M seed): `baseline RSS 51 MB` -> `audit_log: 3000000 rows in 4561ms — RSS 1462 MB, heapUsed 1272 MB`. One table alone exceeds the 1 GB worker mem_limit, which I re-read at infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:269 (`mem_limit: ${WORKER_MEM_LIMIT:-1g}`) with no NODE_OPTIONS/--max-old-space-size anywhere in infra or package.json. READ export-processors.ts:384-401 — the MAX_EXPORT_ROWS check is genuinely after `await client.query(`SELECT * FROM "name"`)`, and `out` retains every table for the whole loop, so the cap is cumulative-after-the-fact. READ worker.ts:44-48 — email, scheduled, import, maintenance and export consumers all live in ONE process, so the OOM does take them all down. CORRECTIONS to the original: (1) 'the export job row is left running forever' is FALSE — apps/api/src/jobs/export-cleanup.job.ts:51-68 reaps `status IN ('running','queued')` rows past a timeout and marks them failed; (2) the crash is not an unbounded loop — the queue is added without `attempts`, so BullMQ's stalled checker re-runs it once (maxStalledCount default 1) and then fails it: two OOM kills, not perpetual. Neither correction touches the mechanism or the severity. Severity kept at blocker: a single tenant click destroys the whole background tier for every tenant, and the 2M-row cap means the top-priced plan can never export its own data.

title: The loans list — and therefore every dashboard load — sequentially scans the entire loans table
what: `loans.list` orders by `[{ loanedAt: 'desc' }, { id: 'desc' }]`. There is no index on `loanedAt` in packages/db-tenant/prisma/schema.prisma (loans has only memberId+status, copyId, dueAt, returnedAt, the customFields GIN and the partial unique on copyId). Postgres therefore reads the whole table and top-N sorts it for a 26-row page. The `overdue` filter (line 798-801) sets `status='active' AND dueAt < now()`; `loans_dueAt_idx` is useless for it because every historical loan has dueAt in the past, so that path also seq-scans.
impact: The tenant home page (apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/page.tsx:51-52) fires TWO of these on every render — `loans?status=active&limit=100` and `loans?overdue=1&limit=100` — plus the reservations list. At the Institutional size the loans heap is 256 MB while production Postgres runs the image default `shared_buffers = 128 MB` (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:320-325 sets only shared_preload_libraries and max_connections). Every dashboard view evicts the entire buffer cache of a Postgres instance shared by all tenants, so one large library degrades every other library on the box. This is the single most frequently hit page in the product.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM loans WHERE 1=1 ORDER BY "loanedAt" DESC, id DESC LIMIT 26` on the 2M-row scale DB: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans (actual rows=666667 loops=3)`, `Buffers: shared hit=485 read=32360`, `Execution Time: 106.786 ms` — 32,845 8 KiB pages (256 MB) touched to return 26 rows, warm. Overdue variant: `Parallel Seq Scan ... Rows Removed by Filter: 661667`, 74.756 ms, 32,845 buffers. Prisma round trip measured at 224 ms wall for the full include (5 queries). `SHOW shared_buffers` = 128MB; `pg_relation_size('loans')` = 256 MB.
fix: Add `@@index([loanedAt(sort: Desc), id(sort: Desc)])` on Loan, and a partial index for the overdue path: `CREATE INDEX loans_active_due ON loans ("dueAt") WHERE "returnedAt" IS NULL` (or `WHERE status = 'active'`). Set `shared_buffers` explicitly on the postgres service (25% of PG_MEM_LIMIT, i.e. 512MB at the current 2g). Replace the dashboard's five list calls with a single cheap counts endpoint (see performance-11).
verification: RAN on libriant_scale. Unfiltered: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans (actual rows=666667 loops=3)`, `Buffers: shared hit=88 read=32757`, `Execution Time: 398.731 ms` cold. `status='active'` (the dashboard's first tile): same 32,845-buffer parallel seq scan, 363 ms. `status='active' AND "dueAt" < now()` (the overdue tile): 32,845 buffers, 58.8 ms warm. `SHOW shared_buffers` = 128MB; `pg_relation_size('loans')` = 256 MB — each of these queries touches twice the whole buffer pool. Confirmed by reading packages/db-tenant/prisma/schema.prisma:381-384 that Loan carries only memberId+status, copyId, dueAt, returnedAt — no loanedAt index, no partial index on the active/overdue predicate, and no index on `status` alone. Severity held at high: two of these fire on every render of the most-visited page in the product.

title: Member-number generation full-scans the members table on every create; the importer makes it quadratic
what: `nextSequenceForYear` runs `client.member.findMany({ where: { memberNumber: { startsWith: 'M-<year>-' } }, select: { memberNumber: true } })` — no `take`, no aggregate — and computes the max in JavaScript. It also omits `archivedAt: null`, so the partial unique index `members_member_number_unique_active` (which carries `WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL`) cannot be used at all. The doc comment at line 32 asserts the opposite: "LIKE is fine here even on big tables because ... the column has a B-tree index via the partial unique index." The import engine calls it once per row (apps/api/src/import/engine/import-engine.ts:489) inside a 5-attempt loop, and each attempt is followed by `member.findFirst({ where: { memberNumber: candidate } })` — again without `archivedAt`, so again a seq scan.
impact: Adding one member to a 100,000-member library costs a full table scan and a 100,000-row transfer into Node. Importing a library's existing roster — the single most important onboarding action for an Institutional customer — is O(n^2): row k pulls k rows, so a 100k-row import moves ~5x10^9 rows. That import will not finish. The same scan also inflates the create transaction, which holds the max_members advisory lock.
evidence: RAN. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) SELECT "memberNumber" FROM members WHERE "memberNumber" LIKE 'M-2026-%'` -> `Seq Scan on members (rows=100000)`, `Buffers: shared hit=2631`. Through Prisma: `nextSequenceForYear('M-2026-'): 100000 rows pulled into Node in 156ms, rss 89MB -> 279MB`. `EXPLAIN` of the importer's follow-up lookup `SELECT id FROM members WHERE "memberNumber"='M-2026-050000' LIMIT 1` -> `Seq Scan on members ... Rows Removed by Filter: 49999`, 1315 buffers; adding `AND "archivedAt" IS NULL` flips it to `Index Scan using members_member_number_unique_active`, 4 buffers, 0.567 ms.
fix: Replace the scan with `SELECT max(...)`: `client.$queryRaw` doing `SELECT max(substring("memberNumber" from '[0-9]+$')::int) FROM members WHERE "memberNumber" LIKE $1` — or better, drop the read-then-write entirely and use a Postgres sequence / a `member_number_counters(year, next)` row with `UPDATE ... RETURNING`. Add `archivedAt: null` to both lookups so the partial unique index is usable, or add a plain `@@index([memberNumber])`. In the importer, seed the counter once in `init()` and increment in memory, exactly as it already does for the quota counter.
verification: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) SELECT "memberNumber" FROM members WHERE "memberNumber" LIKE 'M-2026-%'` on libriant_scale: `Seq Scan on members (actual rows=100000)`, `Buffers: shared read=2631`, 30.6 ms — and `select count(*) ... like 'M-2026-%'` = 100000, i.e. the whole table is transferred into Node. READ member-numbers.ts:39-42 — the findMany has no `take`, no aggregate and no `archivedAt` filter, and `\di members*` confirms the only member-number index is `members_member_number_unique_active`, which is partial on `archivedAt IS NULL` and therefore unusable. The doc comment at line 32-33 asserting the column 'has a B-tree index via the partial unique index' is wrong. Importer path confirmed: import-engine.ts:445 `const memberNumber = number || (await this.generateMemberNumber())` and :486-497 loop nextSequenceForYear + an archivedAt-less findFirst, up to 5 attempts; apps/api/src/import/import.constants.ts:18 sets IMPORT_MAX_ROWS = 250_000, so a 100k-row roster import is permitted and is genuinely O(n^2). ONE NARROWING: generateMemberNumber only runs for rows whose CSV omits memberNumber — an import that carries the library's existing numbers is unaffected. Severity held at high: onboarding a roster is the first thing an Institutional customer does, and 'nothing happens for hours' is how it presents.

title: pinWorkerConnLimit() is a no-op, and the API's own ceiling is 250 connections against max_connections=200
what: `pinWorkerConnLimit` appends `connection_limit=1` to the tenant URL. That parameter is understood by Prisma's old Rust engine, not by `pg`. Under Prisma 7 driver adapters the pool size comes solely from `new PrismaPg({ connectionString, max })` (packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55), so the query string is silently ignored and the pool stays at `TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX` (default 5, packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:21). Four cron jobs — fine-accrual, member-notifications, reservation-expiry, book-metadata-refresh — document this as their mitigation for 'PER-JOB-TENANTPRISMA-CONN-MULTIPLY'. Independently, the API's ceiling is `TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE` (default 50, apps/api/src/config/env.ts:288) x 5 = 250 connections, against `max_connections=200` (infra/compose/docker-compose.prod.yml:325). pgbouncer does not help: it is configured with a single `DB_NAME: libriant_control` (line 349) and tenant URLs are derived from `PG_SUPERUSER_URL: ...@postgres:5432` (line 87, apps/api/src/provisioning/tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104), i.e. every tenant connection bypasses the pooler and hits Postgres directly.
impact: The connection budget the code believes it has does not exist. Past roughly 40 concurrently-active libraries the API alone can exhaust max_connections; Postgres then refuses new backends and every tenant sees 'too many clients already'. Because the pooler only fronts the control DB, there is no layer that can absorb the burst. This is invisible in a 5-tenant pilot and arrives all at once as the tenant count grows.
evidence: RAN. Built a client from the exact URL the jobs use (`postgresql://.../libriant_scale?connection_limit=1`), issued 20 concurrent queries, and counted `pg_stat_activity WHERE datname='libriant_scale'`: `open connections with connection_limit=1 in the URL: 5 (expected 1 if the pin worked)`. A control run without the parameter also gave 5, and idle sockets closed after ~10 s (pg's default idleTimeoutMillis), confirming `max` — not the URL — is what governs. Read: compose grep for the numbers above.
fix: Delete `pinWorkerConnLimit` and pass `makeTenantPrismaClient({ databaseUrl, maxPoolSize: 1 })` in the worker (the option already exists and is honoured), or set `TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX=1` in the worker service's environment. Independently, make the API's ceiling arithmetic explicit: either raise `max_connections`, drop `TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE x TENANT_DB_POOL_MAX` below it, or route tenant DBs through pgbouncer as well (an `[databases] * = host=postgres` wildcard entry in a mounted pgbouncer.ini — all locking in the codebase is `pg_advisory_xact_lock`, so transaction pooling is safe; see performance-17).
verification: PROVED the no-op directly. Built three clients against libriant_scale and counted `pg_stat_activity` while 20 concurrent `SELECT 1 FROM pg_sleep(0.5)` were in flight: `URL connection_limit=1 -> 5 tenant connections`; `no param (default max) -> 5`; `maxPoolSize:1 option -> 1`. So the query-string parameter is ignored and only `PrismaPg({max})` (packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55-58) governs — pinWorkerConnLimit (fine-accrual.job.ts:36-40) is decorative, and the PER-JOB-TENANTPRISMA-CONN-MULTIPLY comment at lines 24-30 documents a mitigation that does not exist. STRENGTHENED: fine-accrual.job.ts:60-72 keeps ONE TenantPrismaService for the whole run and only destroys it in the `finally`, so a sweep holds min(activeTenants, TENANT_CLIENT_CACHE_SIZE=50) x 5 connections for its entire duration, and fine-accrual + member-notifications + book-metadata-refresh + reservation-pickup-expiry can overlap. Arithmetic re-read and confirmed: env.ts:288 cache 50, client.ts:21 pool 5, compose line 325 max_connections=200. pgbouncer cannot absorb it — compose:36 points CONTROL_DATABASE_URL at pgbouncer but :87 PG_SUPERUSER_URL at postgres:5432 directly, and tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-109 `urlForDb()` derives every tenant URL from it by swapping only the path. High.

title: Every book create counts the whole catalogue while holding a per-tenant advisory lock
what: `BooksService.create` opens a transaction, calls `quota.enforceWithinTx` which takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock('quota:<tenant>:max_books:')` (apps/api/src/customization/quota.service.ts:63) and then runs `tx.book.count({ where: { archivedAt: null } })`. There is no index that can answer that count, so it is a full scan of `books`. The lock key is per-tenant, so all concurrent book creates for that library serialize behind it. `update` does the same on un-archive (books.service.ts:360). Members have the identical shape (members.service.ts:233, 366).
impact: At 400,000 titles a single book create takes >113 ms of pure counting and 78 MB of buffer traffic, and the advisory lock caps the tenant at roughly 8 book creates per second no matter how many librarians are working. During a cataloguing session with barcode scanning the whole library's write path stalls, and the count evicts the shared buffer cache for every other tenant on the box. It also puts the create within reach of Prisma's 5 s interactive-transaction timeout once the table is cold.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL` on the 400k-book DB: `Parallel Seq Scan on books (rows=130667 loops=3)`, `Buffers: shared hit=955 read=9028`, `Execution Time: 113.207 ms`. Members equivalent: `Seq Scan on members`, 2631 buffers, 14.056 ms. Read: the count runs strictly after the advisory lock (quota.service.ts:63-65) and inside the same transaction as the insert.
fix: Keep a maintained counter instead of counting: a `resource_counters(feature, count)` row in the tenant DB (or `tenants.bookCount` in the control plane) updated in the same transaction as the insert/archive, with the advisory lock guarding the counter row rather than a scan. Failing that, add `CREATE INDEX books_active ON books (id) WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL` so the count becomes an index-only scan, and shorten the lock window by counting before acquiring it and re-checking cheaply inside.
verification: Code CONFIRMED: quota.service.ts:63-65 takes `pg_advisory_xact_lock` and only then calls `input.count()`, and books.service.ts:203-207 passes `tx.book.count({where:{archivedAt:null}})` inside the same interactive transaction as the insert. Found an AGGRAVATOR the finding missed: the route also runs QuotaInterceptor (apps/api/src/plans/quota.interceptor.ts:19,33 -> countUsage/QUOTA_COUNTERS), so a book create pays the full count TWICE. But two of the finding's numbers do not survive: warm, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) SELECT count(*) FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL` is `Parallel Seq Scan`, 9,983 buffers, `Execution Time: 31.594 ms` (the quoted 113 ms was a cold-cache figure), so the advisory lock caps the tenant near 30 creates/sec, not 8; and 30-60 ms is nowhere near Prisma's 5 s interactive-transaction timeout, so 'puts the create within reach of' that timeout is not supported. The members count is 9.8 ms. No bulk path uses this — import-engine.ts tracks quota with an in-memory `quotaUsed` counter. Remaining real harm: ~156 MB of buffer traffic per interactive book create at plan-max size, evicting a 128 MB shared_buffers pool shared by every tenant. Medium.

title: Six append-only tables have no retention sweep at all; the promised audit-retention job does not exist
what: The tenant schema states audit retention is 'governed by the tenant's plan (`audit_log_retention_days` feature) and enforced by a background job'. No such job exists: `apps/api/src/jobs/registry.ts` lists nine jobs and none of them prunes anything, and a repo-wide grep for 'retention' finds only the plan-feature definition (packages/shared/src/features.ts:113), the seed values (7 / 90 / 365 / 1095 / 3650 / 1e9 days) and a comment in apps/site/src/plans.ts:232 admitting 'nothing prunes audit rows'. The same is true of control-plane `email_outbox` (which stores the full `bodyMarkdown` of every message), `audit_log`, `announcement_deliveries`, `stripe_webhook_events` and `support_redemption_attempts` — the only deleteMany calls in the codebase are `bookAuthor` link replacement and `importRowIssue` cleanup.
impact: Tenant DBs grow without bound on a single shared volume, and the largest table is the one with the least value. Concretely: audit_log is what OOM-kills the exporter (performance-01), and it is 609 MB with 3M rows. email_outbox is worse per unit time — with overdue reminders on, the hourly sweep enqueues one row per overdue loan per day (15,000/day measured), each carrying a full message body, into the *shared* control database. Customers were sold a retention figure (7 days on the entry plan) that the product does not honour, so the plan feature is also a false claim.
evidence: READ: schema.prisma:21 and :563 promise the job; `ls apps/api/src/jobs/` and registry.ts:23-80 show it absent; `grep -rn 'retention' apps packages scripts --include=*.ts` returns only definitions and the apps/site/src/plans.ts:232 admission. RAN: on the scale DB `pg_total_relation_size` gives audit_log 609 MB (289 MB heap + 319 MB indexes) at 3M rows — the largest object in the tenant database, larger than loans.
fix: Add an `audit-retention` cron that, per tenant, resolves `audit_log_retention_days` from EffectivePlanService and runs a chunked `DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE "occurredAt" < $cutoff LIMIT 10000` loop (or partitions audit_log by month and drops partitions). Add equivalent sweeps for email_outbox (delete `sent`/`failed` rows older than N days), announcement_deliveries, stripe_webhook_events and support_redemption_attempts. Until a sweep exists, remove `audit_log_retention_days` from the published plan table.
verification: Growth claim CONFIRMED: `grep -rn retention apps packages scripts` returns only feature definitions, plan seeds and the plans.ts comment — no pruning code; registry.ts:23-80 lists the nine jobs and none prunes a data table; the only `deleteMany` calls in apps/api/src are bookAuthor link replacement (books.service.ts:365, import-engine.ts:340) and importRowIssue cleanup (import-worker.ts:68). audit_log measured at 609 MB / 3M rows, the largest object in the tenant DB. EmailOutbox confirmed unpruned (email-worker.ts only updates status, never deletes) and member-notifications.job.ts:275-278 keys the overdue reminder on `dayKey(now)`, so it really does write one full-body row per overdue loan per day into the shared control DB. TWO CLAIMS REFUTED. (1) 'Customers were sold a retention figure ... so the plan feature is also a false claim' is false: apps/site/src/plans.ts:220-235 deliberately omits audit_log_retention_days from the published pricing table, naming this exact reason ('nothing prunes audit rows, so a printed retention figure would be an unenforced restriction'), and `grep audit_log_retention_days apps/web apps/api/src` returns nothing — the figure is never shown to a customer. (2) 'none of them prunes anything' overstates: export-file-cleanup (registry.ts:45-49) does prune export artifacts and reaps stale job rows. Also worth recording for whoever writes the fix: EmailOutbox.idempotencyKey is `@unique` and IS the dedup mechanism (schema.prisma:754), so deleting sent rows re-arms duplicate sends and needs a separate dedup ledger. Unbounded disk growth on a shared volume, no false customer claim — medium.

title: Hourly overdue sweeps scan the whole loans table, buffer every row, then do N+1 round trips per row
what: `accrueOneTenant` runs an unbounded `client.loan.findMany({ where: { status: 'active', dueAt: { lt: now } } })` and then, for each row, issues `loan.findUnique` + `fine.findFirst` and usually a `fine.updateMany` — three sequential round trips per loan, on a pool the code believes has one connection (see performance-06). `sendMemberNotifications` (apps/api/src/jobs/member-notifications.job.ts:244) runs the identical unbounded scan hourly and then calls `emails.enqueue()` serially per row; when the message already exists, `enqueue` costs a failed INSERT (P2002) plus a `findUniqueOrThrow` against the control DB (apps/api/src/email/email.service.ts:96-120). Neither sweep has a `take`; both jobs iterate every active tenant sequentially in one tick.
impact: For each Institutional tenant, every hour: a 32,845-page seq scan of loans, ~15,000 rows buffered in Node, ~45,000 sequential queries against the tenant DB (fine accrual) and ~30,000 against the shared control DB (notifications, of which ~29,000 are dedup misses that produce nothing). Because the amount changes at every day boundary, the fine `updateMany` fires for every overdue loan once a day. Tenants are processed sequentially, so the hourly tick's duration grows linearly with tenant count and with each library's overdue backlog — and reservation-pickup-expiry, announcement-publish and support-session-expiry are trying to run on 60-second ticks in the same worker.
evidence: RAN against the scale DB. `fine-accrual: overdue findMany -> 15000 rows in 233ms`; sampled the per-row work: `500 loans x 2 reads = 152ms (0.30 ms/loan)` -> `extrapolated for 15000 overdue loans (read-only, no writes) = 4.6s` on a loopback socket, before any writes. `member-notifications overdue: 15000 rows in 309ms (all buffered in memory)`. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS)` of the shared predicate: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans ... Rows Removed by Filter: 661667`, 32,757 buffers, 75.978 ms.
fix: Add the partial index from performance-02 so the sweep seeks instead of scanning. Page the sweep (`take: 500` + keyset cursor) instead of buffering. Collapse the per-row N+1 into set operations: one `fine.findMany({ where: { loanId: { in: batchIds }, status: 'outstanding' } })` per batch, then `createMany`/bulk `UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...)`. In the notification job, pre-filter with a single `emailOutbox.findMany({ where: { idempotencyKey: { in: keys } } })` so duplicates never reach the failed-insert path, and process tenants with bounded concurrency rather than strictly sequentially.
verification: READ fine-accrual.job.ts:95-98 — `client.loan.findMany({where:{status:'active',dueAt:{lt:now}}})` with no `take`, then lines 100-140 do `loan.findUnique` + `fine.findFirst` + `fine.updateMany`/`create` per row. member-notifications.job.ts:244-256 is the same unbounded findMany plus a serial `emails.enqueue()` per row. Predicate cost re-measured: `Parallel Seq Scan on loans`, 32,845 buffers, 58.8 ms warm for the overdue filter (see performance-02). Both sweeps iterate every active tenant sequentially in one tick (fine-accrual.job.ts:61). ONE NARROWING, which is why this stays medium and not high: both are gated on tenant settings that default OFF — schema.prisma:135 `overdueFinesEnabled @default(false)`, :159/:162/:163 `notifyDueSoon/notifyOverdue/notifyHoldReady @default(false)` — and fine-accrual returns at line 89 before the scan when fines are off. The cost only appears for libraries that switch these on, which any real library eventually will. Medium.

title: Dashboard tiles derive counts from list page sizes, buying two full table scans for numbers that are wrong
what: `safeCount` calls a list endpoint and returns `res.items.length` — the page size, not a total. The tiles request `loans?status=active&limit=100`, `loans?overdue=1&limit=100` and `reservations?status=queued&limit=100`, and the service clamps limit to 100 anyway. So the dashboard pays for two full seq scans of the loans table (performance-02) and a full sort of the hold queue (performance-10) on every render, to display a number that saturates at 100.
impact: The most-visited page in the app is also the most expensive query it can issue, and the answer it renders is wrong for any library with more than 100 active loans. Server-rendered, so it re-runs on every navigation to the tenant home, per user.
evidence: READ page.tsx:28-53 (`return { count: res.items.length, error: false }` with the comment 'Cursor-paged endpoints don't return a total; render the page-1 size ... a totals endpoint can replace this later'), and the `Math.min(100, ...)` clamps in loans.service.ts:793 / reservations.service.ts:424. RAN: the two loans queries measured at 106.8 ms and 74.8 ms, 32,845 buffers each (performance-02).
fix: Add one `/t/:slug/summary` endpoint returning real counts from indexed aggregates (`SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='active'), count(*) FILTER (WHERE status='active' AND "dueAt" < now()) FROM loans` backed by the partial index from performance-02), cache it in Redis for 30-60 s, and have the dashboard call that once instead of five list endpoints.
verification: READ apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/page.tsx:28-54 and confirmed verbatim: `safeCount` returns `res.items.length`, and the six parallel calls include `loans?status=active&limit=100`, `loans?overdue=1&limit=100` and `reservations?status=queued&limit=100`. Both loans calls were measured as 32,845-buffer parallel seq scans (363 ms and 59 ms, see performance-02), so every server-rendered visit to the tenant home costs two full scans of a 256 MB table. ADDITIONAL, worse than the finding says: the books and members tiles use `limit=1`, so a 400,000-title catalogue renders its tile as the page-1 size of 1. The number is not merely capped at 100, it is 1. Medium.

title: A one- or two-character search term seq-scans the whole catalogue; nothing enforces a minimum length server-side
what: `if (opts.q) where.searchText = { contains: normalizeText(opts.q) }` renders as `searchText LIKE '%q%'`. The `books_search_trgm` / `members_search_trgm` GIN indexes accelerate that only when the pattern yields at least one full trigram, i.e. from three characters. For one or two characters the planner falls back to a full sequential scan. No minimum is enforced in the DTO or the service (the Combobox has a client-side `minQueryChars`, but the catalog and members search boxes go through DataTable's URL-driven search, which does not).
impact: Typing two letters into the catalogue search and pressing enter costs a 400,000-row seq scan; on the members screen it costs 100,000 rows. In Greek this is a realistic query (single-word stems, and users searching by initials), and it is trivially repeatable — an authenticated staff user can hold the shared Postgres at 100% CPU with a search box.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM books WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND "searchText" LIKE '%ab%' ORDER BY "sortTitle", id LIMIT 26`: `Parallel Seq Scan on books (actual time=112.111..112.111 rows=0 loops=3)`, `Buffers: shared hit=1199 read=8858`. The 16-character control query on the same column used `Bitmap Index Scan on books_search_trgm`, 1371 buffers, 14 ms.
fix: Reject or ignore `q` shorter than three characters in the DTO for books, members and collection records (return an empty page with a 'keep typing' hint), and enforce the same `minQueryChars` in DataTable's search box so the request is never made.
verification: REPRODUCED precisely on libriant_scale. `... WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND "searchText" LIKE '%ab%' ORDER BY "sortTitle", id LIMIT 26` -> `Parallel Seq Scan on books`, `Buffers: shared hit=4950 read=5107` (10,057 buffers). The same query with a three-character term -> `Bitmap Heap Scan on books` via books_search_trgm, `Buffers: shared hit=4 read=3` (7 buffers). A 1,400x difference at the two/three-character boundary, exactly as claimed. No server-side floor exists: books.controller.ts:44,53 passes `q` straight through whenever `q.length` is non-zero, and books.dto.ts has no query DTO with a `@Length` on it. Rate limiting does not cover this — `RateLimitService` is wired only into auth.controller.ts, admin-auth.controller.ts, password-reset.service.ts, email-verification.service.ts and applications.service.ts; no list or search route touches it, and infra/caddy/Caddyfile has no rate_limit directive. Medium.

title: Prisma cursor pagination degrades linearly with page depth on every list endpoint
what: Every list method pages with `cursor: { id: after }, skip: 1` while ordering by a non-unique column plus id (books: sortTitle+id; members: sortName+id; loans: loanedAt+id; audit: occurredAt+id; reservations: status+queuePosition+placedAt+id). Prisma renders that as `WHERE (sortTitle = (SELECT sortTitle FROM books WHERE id = $1) AND id >= (SELECT ...)) OR (sortTitle > (SELECT ...))`. The OR-of-subselects is not a btree start-key, so Postgres scans the index from the beginning of the range and discards every row before the cursor. Page N costs O(N x pageSize), and walking the whole list is O(n^2).
impact: A librarian paging through a 400,000-title catalogue gets progressively slower pages, and the API burns whole-index scans doing it. It is not just a UI annoyance: the offline/PWA sync, the desktop app and any script that walks a list page-by-page pay quadratic cost against the shared Postgres.
evidence: RAN. Captured the exact SQL from Prisma's query event log, then EXPLAIN ANALYZE'd it. Page ~8,000 of books: `Index Scan using "books_sortTitle_idx" ... Rows Removed by Filter: 200000`, `Buffers: shared hit=40 read=5951 written=1331`, `Execution Time: 86.872 ms`. Last page: `Rows Removed by Filter: 399000`, `Execution Time: 190.272 ms`. Page 1 of the same query: 13 ms. The same OR-of-subselects shape was captured for members, loans and audit_log.
fix: Stop using Prisma's `cursor`. Encode the cursor as the tuple of the sort keys (`sortTitle|id`, base64) and emit a true row-value predicate — `WHERE ("sortTitle", id) > ($1, $2)` via `$queryRaw` or `Prisma.sql` — which a `@@index([sortTitle, id])` can seek directly. Add the composite indexes to match each list's orderBy.
verification: Mechanism REPRODUCED exactly. Captured Prisma's emitted SQL from the query event log for `book.findMany({cursor:{id},skip:1, orderBy:[sortTitle,id]})`: it is the OR-of-subselects the finding describes. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) of that literal SQL at depth 200,000: `Index Scan using "books_sortTitle_idx"`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 204082`, `Buffers: shared hit=6120`, `Execution Time: 32.254 ms`. So the O(depth) cost is real. IMPACT REFUTED. The finding claims 'the offline/PWA sync, the desktop app and any script that walks a list page-by-page pay quadratic cost'. There is no such consumer: grepping apps/web and apps/desktop for `nextCursor`/`after` returns only apps/web/components/DataTable.tsx (the 'Load more' button) and Combobox; apps/web/lib/offline-queue.ts is a write replay queue for circulation actions (checkout/return/renew/mark-lost), it syncs no lists. Reaching depth 200k in the UI takes ~8,000 clicks at 25 rows a page; at a realistic depth of 50 pages the filter discards ~1,250 rows, which is unmeasurable. Real defect, no realistic harm — low.

title: book-metadata-refresh full-scans the catalogue every 6 hours and can never finish a pass
what: The candidate query orders by `metadataRefreshedAt ASC NULLS FIRST`. `books_metadataRefreshedAt_idx` is a plain ascending btree, which in Postgres is NULLS LAST, so the index cannot satisfy the ordering and the planner falls back to a full scan plus top-N sort. It scans 400,000 rows to return `PER_TENANT_LIMIT = 40` (line 35), and the job ticks every 6 hours (registry.ts:59-60), i.e. 160 books/day per tenant.
impact: Four full scans of every tenant's books table per day, each producing 40 useful rows. Worse, the feature cannot converge: at 160 books/day a 400,000-title catalogue needs over 6,800 days for one pass, while `REFRESH_INTERVAL_DAYS = 30` makes rows eligible again after a month. An Institutional library's catalogue will never be enriched, so the cost buys nothing.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of the exact SQL captured from Prisma's query log: `Parallel Seq Scan on books (actual rows=130667 loops=3)`, `Rows Removed by Filter: 2667`, `Sort Key: "metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST`, `Buffers: shared hit=931 read=9124`, `Execution Time: 34.847 ms`; Prisma wall time 118 ms. Read: PER_TENANT_LIMIT=40 at line 35, 6 h interval at registry.ts:59.
fix: Change the index to match the sort — `CREATE INDEX books_metadata_refresh ON books ("metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST) WHERE "archivedAt" IS NULL AND isbn13 IS NOT NULL` — and add the 'still missing a field' condition to the partial predicate so the index is a work queue rather than a table scan. Then either raise the per-tenant budget so a pass can actually complete, or make the job event-driven (enqueue a refresh when a book is created/imported without metadata) and drop the sweep.
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED: `pg_indexes` shows `books_metadataRefreshedAt_idx ... btree ("metadataRefreshedAt")` (plain ASC = NULLS LAST) while book-metadata-refresh.job.ts:118 asks for `nulls: 'first'`; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE,BUFFERS) of the real predicate gives `Parallel Seq Scan on books`, `Sort Key: "metadataRefreshedAt" NULLS FIRST`, `Buffers: shared hit=4660 read=5395`, `Execution Time: 74.541 ms`. But the severity does not follow. The job runs every 6 h (registry.ts:59-60), so this is four 75 ms scans per tenant per day — about 300 ms of scanning a day, against a dashboard that does 2 x 32,845 buffers on every single page view. The convergence arithmetic is also wrong: PER_TENANT_LIMIT=40 x 4 runs = 160 books/day, and 400,000/160 = 2,500 days, not the 'over 6,800 days' claimed. The non-convergence is a product/feature-design problem, not a performance one, and the candidate set is much smaller than 400k (only books with an isbn13 still missing a backfillable field). Low.

title: The reservations list sorts every live hold in the library to render 26 rows
what: The default list has no bookId/memberId filter and orders by `status ASC, queuePosition ASC NULLS LAST, placedAt DESC, id ASC`. The only reservation index that could help is `reservations_bookId_status_queuePosition_idx`, whose leading column is bookId — unusable without that filter. Nothing indexes `(status, queuePosition, placedAt, id)`, so Postgres seq-scans the table and sorts the whole live set for each page.
impact: Page latency scales with the size of the hold queue rather than the page size, and the four-key ordering makes performance-03's cursor problem worse (the OR-of-subselects predicate is built over the leading key only). The holds screen is the second-most-used circulation view after loans.
evidence: RAN `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT id FROM reservations WHERE status IN ('queued','ready') ORDER BY status ASC, "queuePosition" ASC NULLS LAST, "placedAt" DESC, id ASC LIMIT 26` with 40,000 live holds: `Seq Scan on reservations (actual rows=40000)`, `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`, `Buffers: shared hit=591`, 9.304 ms. Prisma wall time 135 ms for the page including the three relation-batch queries.
fix: Add `@@index([status, queuePosition, placedAt, id])` on Reservation so the default ordering is an index scan, and keyset-paginate on that tuple (performance-03).
verification: Mechanism CONFIRMED: reservations.service.ts:429-439 orders by status, queuePosition NULLS LAST, placedAt desc, id; `pg_indexes` on reservations shows nothing leading with `status`, only `reservations_bookId_status_queuePosition_idx`. RAN the query at 40,000 live holds (35,000 queued + 5,000 ready): `Seq Scan on reservations (actual rows=40000)`, `Sort Method: top-N heapsort`, `Buffers: shared hit=14 read=583`, `Execution Time: 14.121 ms`. That is the whole harm: 4.7 MB and 14 ms at a hold-queue size (40,000 simultaneous live holds for a 100,000-member library) that is already far beyond anything a real library sees. At a plausible few hundred live holds the scan is sub-millisecond. Real missing index, negligible cost — low.

title: No statement_timeout or query timeout is configured anywhere for tenant traffic
what: The postgres service's command sets only `shared_preload_libraries` and `max_connections` — no `statement_timeout`, no `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, no `lock_timeout`. `makeTenantPrismaClient` passes only `{ connectionString, max }` to `PrismaPg` (packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55), and the control client passes only `{ connectionString }` (packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34, so it also inherits pg's default pool of 10 rather than a deliberate figure). The only place a statement timeout is set is the export worker (export-processors.ts:29). NestJS sets no HTTP handler timeout in main.ts either.
impact: A runaway query — a two-character search over a cold 400k catalogue, a stuck lock wait, a pathological trigram scan — occupies one of the five per-tenant pool slots for as long as it takes, with nothing to shed it. Five such queries wedge that library entirely, and the requests behind them queue in pg's connection pool with no acquire deadline. There is no automatic recovery; an operator has to `pg_terminate_backend` by hand.
evidence: READ: compose command block lines 320-325; packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55-59 and packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34 show the full option set passed to PrismaPg; grep for `statement_timeout` across apps/ packages/ infra/ returns only export-processors.ts. I attempted to demonstrate unbounded pool queueing empirically and could not reproduce it cleanly in a single process, so the impact statement above is derived from configuration, not measured.
fix: Add `-c statement_timeout=30s -c idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=60s -c lock_timeout=5s` to the postgres command (with the export/import/migration paths raising it per-session where they legitimately need longer), and give the control client an explicit `max` so its budget is deliberate.
verification: Every configuration fact re-verified. docker-compose.prod.yml:320-325 passes only `-c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements -c max_connections=200`. `grep -rn 'statement_timeout|idle_in_transaction|lock_timeout' apps packages infra scripts` returns only export-processors.ts:337/345/370 (the export worker's own 60 s cap) and two DR-drill scripts. packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55-58 passes `{connectionString, max}` and packages/db-control/src/client.ts:33 passes `{connectionString}` alone, so the control client does inherit pg's default pool of 10. main.ts installs only cookieParser and the exception filter — no HTTP timeout. Kept at low and kept honest: the finding already states its impact is derived from configuration, not measured, and I did not reproduce it either. It earns its place only because performance-01/-02/-12 show queries that can run long enough for the absence to matter.

title: API responses are served uncompressed from the app host
what: `encode zstd gzip` appears only inside the `{$SITE_HOST}` block (the marketing site). Neither the `{$PUBLIC_HOST}` block (line 149) nor the `{$ADMIN_HOST}` block (line 205) has an `encode` directive, and `apps/api/src/main.ts` installs no compression middleware — the only `app.use` calls are `cookieParser()` and the exception filter. So everything under `/lbr-api/*` leaves the origin uncompressed.
impact: Mostly absorbed for browsers by Cloudflare's edge compression, so the user-visible cost is limited — but origin-to-edge egress and the desktop/PWA sync paths pay full size, and a self-hosted or direct-to-origin deployment would ship the raw bytes to the client.
evidence: RAN: serialised the real DTO shapes from the scale DB. `GET /loans?limit=100` = 60.9 KiB raw / 4.0 KiB gzip (93% saved); `GET /catalog/books?limit=25` = 15.7 KiB raw / 1.4 KiB gzip. READ: Caddyfile blocks at 149, 205, 253-264; main.ts:29-45.
fix: Add `encode zstd gzip` to the `{$PUBLIC_HOST}` and `{$ADMIN_HOST}` site blocks (one line each), or install `compression` middleware in main.ts.
verification: `grep -n encode infra/caddy/Caddyfile` returns exactly one hit, line 264, inside the SITE_HOST block. Re-read the PUBLIC_HOST block (line 149) and the ADMIN_HOST block (line 205) in full — neither has an `encode` directive, and both reverse_proxy to api:3001 for /lbr-api/*. `grep -n 'app.use|compression' apps/api/src/main.ts` returns only line 39 `app.use(cookieParser())`. Low is the right rating: the finding is candid that Cloudflare's edge compression absorbs most of it for browsers, and the residual cost is origin egress plus direct-to-origin clients.

title: Hourly storage sweep recursively walks every tenant's entire flat file tree
what: The sweep loops every active tenant and calls `driver.sweepStaleTemps`, which recurses the whole storage root with `fs.readdir(dir, { withFileTypes: true })` (apps/api/src/storage/drivers/local-driver.ts:199-228). Refs are flat within a resource folder (`covers/<id>.jpg`, `members/<id>.jpg`), so an Institutional tenant ends up with a single directory holding hundreds of thousands of entries, and readdir materialises every Dirent into one array. It runs hourly (registry.ts:70-79) even though, as the job's own comment notes, temps only appear after a crash mid-upload — the working set is normally empty.
impact: Hourly, per tenant, the worker allocates and discards an array of every file the library owns and stats the shared storage volume for nothing. It competes for the same worker process and the same disk as exports and imports.
evidence: READ: storage-temp-cleanup.job.ts:26-41 (loop over all active tenants), local-driver.ts:199-228 (unfiltered recursive readdir with withFileTypes, recursing into every directory), registry.ts:70-79 (60-minute interval). Ref layout confirmed from covers.controller.ts / photos.controller.ts usage of `covers/<id>` and `members/<id>`.
fix: Confine the sweep to a dedicated `_tmp/` staging directory (write temps there and rename into place), so the walk is O(orphans) instead of O(files). Drop the interval to daily. Shard the resource directories by id prefix (`covers/ab/abcd....jpg`) so no directory holds 400k entries.
verification: READ storage-temp-cleanup.job.ts:25-41 (loops every active tenant, hourly per registry.ts:70-79) and local-driver.ts:199-228 — `fs.readdir(dir, {withFileTypes:true})` recursing unconditionally into every directory with no prefix filter and no depth bound. ONE CORRECTION: it does NOT stat every file. `withFileTypes` supplies the type from getdents, and `fs.stat` runs only for names matching `/\.tmp-[0-9a-f]+$/i` (isTempUpload, line 190) — so the cost is one Dirent array per directory plus the syscalls, not a stat storm. That is the whole harm: an hourly allocate-and-discard of an array of every file the library owns, for a working set that is normally empty by the job's own comment. Low.

title: Production Postgres is initialised with el_GR.UTF-8, so no prefix-LIKE can use a btree and every large sort pays libc collation
what: `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` is set on the postgres service and no `POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS` overrides it, so every database in the cluster is created with the el_GR.UTF-8 collation. Two consequences: (a) `LIKE 'prefix%'` cannot use an ordinary btree index — that needs `text_pattern_ops` (or a C-collation column), and no such index exists anywhere in either schema, so `nextSequenceForYear`'s `startsWith` (performance-04) has no index path even after the `archivedAt` fix; (b) all `ORDER BY sortTitle / sortName` comparisons go through libc `strcoll` rather than `memcmp`, which is several times slower per comparison on the large sorts identified in performance-02, -09 and -10.
impact: Every timing in this report is optimistic. The audit environment initdb's with `--locale=C` (docs/audit/pre-release-2026-08-23/env/setup-audit-env.sh:22), so the measured plans used the fastest possible comparator; production will be slower on exactly the queries that are already the slowest.
evidence: READ docker-compose.prod.yml:315-319 (no POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS) and setup-audit-env.sh:22 (`initdb ... --locale=C`). RAN: `\d+ members` / `pg_indexes` on both schemas — no index uses `text_pattern_ops` or `COLLATE "C"`; the `LIKE 'M-2026-%'` plan is `Seq Scan` even under the C locale because the predicate matches every row.
fix: The sort/search columns are already accent-folded and lowercased by the application, so their collation carries no linguistic meaning — declare them `@db.Text` with `COLLATE "C"` (a migration `ALTER TABLE books ALTER COLUMN "sortTitle" TYPE text COLLATE "C"`, likewise sortName, searchText, memberNumber, barcode) and rebuild their indexes. Re-measure performance-02/-04/-09/-10 afterwards against an el_GR cluster, not the C-locale audit box.
verification: Config facts CONFIRMED: docker-compose.prod.yml:319 sets `LANG: el_GR.UTF-8` with no POSTGRES_INITDB_ARGS, and the audit cluster is C (`\l` shows Collate=C for every database). Both consequences are weaker than stated. (a) The prefix-LIKE claim is a true Postgres behaviour, but the finding itself concedes the only prefix-LIKE in the codebase (`nextSequenceForYear`) seq-scans for an unrelated reason (it matches every row, and its partial index is unusable) — so no query path is demonstrably harmed by it, before or after the performance-04 fix. (b) 'several times slower per comparison' is unverified and probably wrong: the production image is postgres:16-alpine, i.e. musl, where strcoll_l is byte comparison regardless of the recorded collation name. I could not test this — docker is not installed on this host, so no el_GR cluster could be built. Worse for the headline claim ('every timing in this report is optimistic'), I found the audit box is PESSIMISTIC in the direction that matters most for a Greek product: under the C locale pg_trgm emits no trigrams for Greek text, so `searchText LIKE '%αβγ%'` and even '%αβγδ%' both fall back to `Parallel Seq Scan`, whereas the ASCII '%abc%' uses the GIN index — production's el_GR locale would make Greek search FASTER than measured here, not slower. Recorded as info: a real environment divergence worth re-measuring on, with no demonstrated defect.

title: Verified: pgbouncer transaction mode is compatible with this code — but it only fronts the control database
what: The brief asked whether anything relies on prepared statements or session-level state under `POOL_MODE: transaction`. Nothing does. Every lock in the codebase is `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (transaction-scoped, released at COMMIT): loans.service.ts:229/418/622, quota.service.ts:63, reservation-expiry.job.ts. There are no LISTEN/NOTIFY, no `SET`/`SET LOCAL`, no temp tables and no explicit PREPARE. `@prisma/adapter-pg` builds its query object with `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)` and neither client factory sets `statementNameGenerator`, so `name` is undefined and every statement is unnamed (no server-side prepared statement to survive a pooled connection swap). Prisma Migrate does take a session-level advisory lock, and it is already routed around the pooler via `PG_SUPERUSER_URL` (scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh:16-24). The one gap is scope: `DB_NAME: libriant_control` gives pgbouncer exactly one database, so no tenant connection is pooled at all — see performance-06.
impact: No defect. Recorded so the compatibility question is closed and so a future change (adding LISTEN/NOTIFY, session GUCs, or a driver that names statements) is known to break the assumption.
evidence: READ: `grep -rn 'advisory|LISTEN|NOTIFY|SET LOCAL|CREATE TEMP|DEALLOCATE|PREPARE ' apps/api/src packages` returns only pg_advisory_xact_lock call sites; `grep -n 'name:' node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+adapter-pg@7.9.1/.../dist/index.js` -> line 655 `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)`; neither packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55 nor packages/db-control/src/client.ts:34 passes that option.
fix: None required for compatibility. When fixing performance-06, a wildcard `[databases] * = host=postgres port=5432` entry (via a mounted pgbouncer.ini rather than the image's DB_NAME shortcut) is safe for tenant traffic given the above.
verification: Spot-checked the two load-bearing claims. `grep -rn statementNameGenerator` in node_modules/.pnpm/@prisma+adapter-pg@7.9.1/.../dist/index.js hits exactly line 655 `name: this.pgOptions?.statementNameGenerator?.(query)`, and neither packages/db-tenant/src/client.ts:55 nor packages/db-control/src/client.ts:33 passes that option — so statements are unnamed and nothing survives a pooled connection swap. The scope gap is confirmed independently: docker-compose.prod.yml:36 routes CONTROL_DATABASE_URL through pgbouncer, :87 sets PG_SUPERUSER_URL to postgres:5432, and tenant-provisioning.service.ts:104-109 `urlForDb()` builds every tenant URL by swapping only the pathname of that superuser URL — so no tenant connection is ever pooled. Kept as info; it closes a question rather than reporting a defect.
